Gibbons open up 1922 by knocking out Pat McCarthy in the fourth round at Boston. A fourth meeting with Harry Greb was arranged for New York's Madison Square Garden over the fifteen round route on March 13th. The Gibbons camp felt that the added weight of Gibbons would tire the smaller Greb over the longer distance. A hug crowd of 11,897 paid a gate of $118,762 to see a great fight. After fifteen rounds of back and forth fighting, it was the aggressive Greb that came away with the official decision. Tommy Gibbons had been handed his first official loss since he started back in 1911. For this match, Gibbons received what was his largest purse to date in this career, $17,500.
Knockout of Harry Foley and Sailor Martin followed. Gibbons felt is was time for a vaction and he took the summer off, returning to the ring on October 13 to meet hometown rival and friend from St. Paul, Billy Miske, in New York's Madison Square Garden. Tommy was a concerned man at the time because during the summer that had just passed, his father, Thomas Sr. had become very ill and was not expected to live. Tommy had he New York commitment however, so he left St. Paul for the meeting with Miske.
Several thousand New Yorkers turned out to see the two superstars from St. Paul cross gloves in the big city, paying out $39, 392 for the privilege. In the seventh round, a telegram came to ringside and was given to manager Eddie Kane. The wire was from Mike Gibbons and contained the news that the elder Gibbons had passed away from stomach cancer. He was 72 years old and strangely enough had never seen either of his two famous sons in the ring.
Kane read the telegram and put it in his pocket, deciding not to tell Tommy until after the fight. Gibbons, however, sensed that something was not right as the fight progressed, affecting his concentration. The fight came to a sudden ending in the tenth round when Billy claimed a foul. The referee agreed and declared Miske the victor handing Gibbons his second official defeat.
Gibbons left New York as soon as he possibly could, returning to St. Paul for his father's funeral. He was back in action though on the 13th of November kayoing George Ashe in one following that ended up with a seven round knockout of Joe Burke in Buffalo on December 11. Four days later Gibbons was back in St. Paul where he won the newspaper decision over his local rival Billy Miske. He started 1923 by scoring three knockouts, Jim Tracy went in two. Andy Schmader in one and veteran Chuck Wiggins was starched in the ten round in New Orleans.
In the Spring of 1923 a small group in the small Montana town of Shelby headed by the mayor, Jim Johnson, came up with an idea of how to publicized their town which was supposed to be rich in oil. Their idea was to stage a world heavyweight championship fight on July 4th in Shelby, featuring champion Jack Dempsey defending his title. Their selection to meet Dempsey was the man considered to be the top contender, Tommy Gibbons of St. Paul
They knew they would need help in not only arranging the fight, but also in promoting it, so the group contacted St. Paul businessman Moses Zimmerman who, in turn, called on Minneapolis promoter Mike Collins. Collins listed to the idea and considered the idea and the Shelby people crazy. After several meeting with Collins, Zimmerman finally persuaded him to make a trip to Shelby -- after a hefty advance payment that is. After meeting with all concerned and looking over the site, Collins finally agreed to join them in the title fight venture.
Returning to St. Paul, Collins contacted Jack Kearns, the manager of Dempsey about the proposed meeting with Gibbons in Shelby. Kearns listened and then told Collins he wanted a purse of $300,000 and training expenses of $150, 0000. Kearns figured with those demands he would never hear from Collins again, After conferring with the people in Shelby, Collins again contracted Kearns with the offer of a $300,000 purse but only $10,000 in training expenses.
A meeting of all concerned parties was held in Chicago at which time Kearns laid his demands on the table. He wanted the entire purse of $300,000 paid before the fight and agreed to a three payment deal; the Shelby group agreed. Now they had to get Gibbons name on a contract so Johnson, Zimmerman, and Collins met with Gibbons and his manager, Eddie Kane in Minnesota. After much discussion Gibbons and Kane accepted a deal of fifty percent of the gate receipts after Dempsey had been paid his $300,000. The promoters figured the gate to be at least a half million which would give Gibbons around $100,000 plus a crack at the title.
With the deal sealed, promotion of the event began. To bring fight fans from around the country to the little town of Shelby, twenty-two trains were arranged for and the word went out about the Dempsey and Gibbons meeting. The first payment of $100,000 plus $10,000 expense were paid to Kearns on time.
Back in St. Paul Gibbons and Kane got their group of sparring partners together and along with Tommy's family, they packed up for the trip to Shelby. At the Union Railroad Station in downtown St. Paul a crowd of $1,500 put on a spectacular going away celebration as Gibbons left for his meeting with the kayo punching Dempsey. Mayor Nelson presented Tommy with a good luck rabbit's foot along with a large floral horseshoe from his many admirers. The tale behind the rabbit's foot, according to Mayor Nelson, was that it was the left hind foot of a buck rabbit, killed at midnight in an Alabama cemetery under a fool moon. Nelson said the foot was given to him by a southern black man and he had very good luck since it came into his possession.

Lithium sulfate is not a replacement for lithium. It's simply another lithium-bearing compound that can potentially be used in certain LFP battery manufacturing processes.

In conventional lithium processing, sulfuric acid can be used to extract lithium from mineral deposits, creating a lithium-bearing sulfate solution. This solution is then purified and processed into battery-grade lithium carbonate or other lithium chemicals.

Lithium sulfate can also potentially serve as a direct precursor in certain LFP manufacturing methods, bypassing some conventional carbonate conversion steps. This could offer processing efficiencies, although commercial adoption depends on costs, purity requirements and manufacturing compatibility.

Most importantly, switching from lithium carbonate to lithium sulfate or lithium dihydrogen phosphate does not reduce the elemental lithium required to manufacture the same quantity of LFP cathode material.

Alternative precursors may change how lithium is processed and purchased, but they don't eliminate underlying lithium demand. The market needs to distinguish between changing lithium chemistry and declining lithium consumption.

By distinguishing biologically produced N₂ from atmospheric nitrogen, the method revealed nitrogen loss that can be missed by traditional approaches across environments ranging from aquifers and lakes to coastal basins, oxygen minimum zones, and marine sediments.

The work offers scientists a new way to better understand the nitrogen cycle — one of the fundamental processes that supports life on Earth.

Palestinian terrorism 🇵🇸

And since honesty is rare in my politics, let me admit a few things.

**1947.** The United Nations offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would “throw the Jews into the sea.” Instead, I lost everything and called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn’t offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

**1948–2025.** The Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps across generations so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and families for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

**1967.** After another war I lost, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza Strip. Instead, I insisted on “no peace, no recognition, no negotiations.” Three no’s. Fifty years later, I still have no state. It turns out that rejection doesn’t pay the rent.

**Oslo, the 1990s.** Israel said: “Let’s try.” It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions of dollars in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

**Gaza, 2005.** Israel withdrew completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into the Singapore of the Mediterranean. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions of dollars in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

**Democracy?** I haven’t held elections for about 20 years. Hamas kills opponents in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they’re too busy fighting over power.

**Religion.** Instead of building a future, I put clerics on television who teach children to hate Jews. I glorify the “martyrs” who blow up buses. I raise my children on songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

**The Arab world.** The Arab regimes call me “brother.” But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, yet they celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

**Absurdity.** I still say I want to “build a state.” And ironically, right next to me sits Israel: the neighbor who built a thriving democracy, a technological power, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no endless wealth—just courage. I could have learned from it, copied it, cooperated with it. Instead, I chose envy and anger.

**Anti-Jewish obsession.** I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: “Two states, two states.” Instead, I keep repeating: “From the river to the sea.” Instead of showing honor, hospitality, and the rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting “peace” to the Israelis, I shouted “death to the Jews.” Then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don’t trust me, when they get angry, disappointed, and convinced that I never want coexistence.

**Responsibility.** I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel’s fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel’s fault. I glorify death more than life? Israel’s fault. Responsibility is not my strength.

I am Palestinian.

I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But I am often a victim of my own leaders, my own decisions, and my own refusal to let go of hatred.

And this, dear reader, is the tragedy that no one wants to acknowledge.

text:
On August 9th Gibbons made his only trip across the ocean for a boxing match. Manger Kane arranged a big fight in London, England with the top heavyweight in England as well as Europe, Jack Bloomfield. Gibbons was guaranteed $50,000 for the Bloomfield match. Tommy sailed off to England to continue his training. Gibbons became extremely popular with the English fans while he was there.
Shortly before the fight, the promoters came to Gibbons and told him that they could not pay him the $50,000 that he was promised; they would only be able to pay $25,000. Gibbons could have refused to fight at that time if he had chosen but said the $25,000 was alright and that he would go on with the fight as planned. It turned out to be as easy outing for Gibbons as he gave the British fans at the outdoor site and Bloomfield, a day to remember as he put on a terrific exhibition of clever boxing, then in the third round showed his punching ability by knocking out Bloomfield.
After seeing a bit of England, the Gibbons entourage boarded the liner Olympic for the trip back to the States. Upon his arrival in New Your he was met by several reporters who main question was why he had fought for only half of what he had been guaranteed. Tommy Gibbons explained, "If we'd been like some American fighters and walked out when we did not get what was coming to us, ti would have meant the end of boxing in England. There has been too much crying about greed for money in the boxing game, particularly abroad where they think American fighters are money made. I could not play them a mean trick by quitting for a few thousand dollars." This was typically Tommy Gibbons.
He returned to the resin pit in October for two bouts, kayoing Bill Reed in three and Ted Jamison in one. A December trip to New York sawn him flatten tough veteran Kid Norfolk in the sixth round before 13,000 customers. He opened 1925 by knocking out Jack Burke in six, three weeks later Tiny Jim Herman bit the dust in three rounds at Detroit.
In March of 1925, Gene Tunney gave Harry Greb a sound pasting in the St. Paul Auditorium. After the fight, Greb told Tunney he was now ready to meet Tommy Gibbons whom Tunney had to defeat to get a crack at Jack Dempsey and the heavyweight title. Tunney and his people went to New York in the hopes or arranging a match with the Gibbons. Offers were made and the thirty-four year old Gibbons knew this was his chance to make some money; he accepted after lengthy talks for a purse of $110,000, his largest payday of his career. The date in New York's Polo Grounds was set for June 5.
Gibbons did most of his training in St. Paul at brother Mike Gibbons' Rose Room Gym in the Hamm Building's lower level where he had plenty of excellent sparring partners to work with. In April of 1925 Tommy's wife Helen entered St. Joseph's Hospital suffering from a nervous breakdown. With a number of children at home and his wife in the hospital, there was plenty of pressure on Tommy as he prepared for the Tunney match. The time arrived for Tommy to go to New York to complete his training so he had to try to leave his problems behind.
A turnout of 23,750 fight fans were on hand at the Polo Grounds to see the top two contenders and boxing masters finally cross gloves. The fight was a close affair until age and 106 previous fights caught up with Tommy Gibbons and Gene Tunney was able to administer the first kayo of Gibbons in the twelfth round. Gibbons knew after the knockout loss that is now time to hand them up but at least he got the lion's share of the $161,166 the fight had drawn.
After the fight, Gibbons met with reporters and told them that he was retiring not only because of the kayo loss, but also due to the serious illness of his wife Helen, who had become ill while he was training fir the Tunney fight. He said he was also influenced by the fact that his brother Mike had lost the sight in his right eye. He was stilly highly-rated and could have continued to make several hundred thousand dollars, however he had decided to retire.
Back home his wife Helen was not told that her husband had suffered the first knockout loss in his career in New York. For her own health she was told his fight had ended in a draw. When Tommy returned home he told his wife the truth about the fight and that he was quitting the ring for good.
[According to Tim Gibbons, Tommy Gibbons' grandson, his grandfather said that he had exactly 106 fights.]
After hanging up the gloves, Gibbons went to work for a major insurance company in St. Paul as an agent. He became highly successful selling millions of dollars of insurance. In 1929 Tommy and his wife made a gift of $50,000 to the Catholic Church to construct a church in Osakis, Minnesota where they had maintained a summer home since 1915. Thanks to the Gibbons' the Church of Immaculate Conception was built there. IN 1930 Pope Pius XI conferred on Gibbons the insignia "Bene Merentl" for conspicuous contributions to citizenship, education, and religion, The insignia was in the form of a gold medallion and presented to Mr. And Mrs. Gibbons at St. Cloud, Minnesota.

Serving more AI interactions requires computing systems built for running AI models. WAKE UP! THE GREATEST DECEPTION MAY NOT BE WHAT HUMANITY HAS BEEN TAUGHT TO BELIEVE, BUT WHAT IT HAS BEEN CONDITIONED NEVER TO QUESTION.

How extraordinarily convenient that billions of human beings have been persuaded to interpret political competition as evidence of institutional independence, as though the existence of opposing parties, competing ideologies, and publicly antagonistic personalities somehow precludes the possibility of shared financial interests, overlapping institutional loyalties, or coordinated objectives among those occupying the highest concentrations of power.

Throughout recorded history, the preservation of authority has depended upon considerably more than military superiority or economic dominance. It has required the cultivation of legitimacy, the management of information, the manipulation of collective perception, and, perhaps most importantly, the ability to persuade populations that the boundaries of their understanding represent the boundaries of reality itself.

For nearly 2,000 years, the expression "panem et circenses," or bread and circuses, has served as a warning about the political usefulness of distraction.

The Roman satirist Juvenal recognized that a population increasingly preoccupied with entertainment and immediate gratification could become progressively disengaged from the political responsibilities necessary to preserve its own independence.

Now consider how profoundly that principle has evolved within a civilization possessing unprecedented capabilities for psychological profiling, behavioral prediction, information manipulation, and technological surveillance.

Humanity has entered an era in which the architecture of influence is becoming increasingly indistinguishable from the infrastructure of everyday existence.

Artificial intelligence can analyze immense quantities of human behavioral data, identify patterns invisible to ordinary observation, and generate increasingly sophisticated predictions concerning individual and collective decision making.

Intelligence agencies possess extensive histories of clandestine operations, covert influence, surveillance, and classified technological development, while governments and private corporations continue investing extraordinary resources into systems capable of collecting, interpreting, and exploiting information about human populations.

And yet, we are expected to assume that the technological capabilities publicly disclosed to ordinary citizens represent the absolute limits of what humanity has developed.

On what intellectual foundation does such an assumption rest...?

The historical record demonstrates that consequential military and intelligence technologies have repeatedly existed within classified environments before becoming publicly acknowledged.

The precise extent of present day technological secrecy remains unknown and conceal the technological realities that are dramatically more advanced, which is precisely why meaningful transparency and independent scrutiny are indispensable.

Now consider the implications of technological asymmetry on a civilizational scale...

What happens when a comparatively small concentration of institutions possesses the computational infrastructure, financial resources, intelligence capabilities, and informational advantages necessary to influence the decisions of populations that cannot independently examine the systems affecting them?

What happens when the mechanisms responsible for shaping public perception become sufficiently sophisticated that individuals begin mistaking externally influenced preferences for independently formed convictions?

And what happens when technologies initially introduced under the justifications of convenience, security, efficiency, and public protection gradually establish the infrastructure necessary for unprecedented concentrations of authority?

The history of authoritarianism, coercive population policies, eugenics, and institutional abuses provides ample reason to examine these possibilities with exceptional seriousness...

Perhaps the most consequential question is not whether humanity possesses the technological capacity to construct increasingly comprehensive systems of control, but whether the institutions developing those systems possess sufficient accountability to prevent their abuse.

Consider the extraordinary psychological contradiction of a civilization that celebrates its unprecedented access to information while simultaneously becoming increasingly dependent upon centralized systems to determine which information it encounters.

We have developed the ability to communicate instantaneously across continents, yet the architecture governing those communications remains largely beyond the comprehension or direct control of the populations relying upon it.

We celebrate technological progress as evidence of expanding human freedom, even as many of the same technological developments create unprecedented opportunities for behavioral monitoring, automated classification, and institutional intervention.

And while these transformations accelerate, public attention remains consumed by an apparently inexhaustible procession of political controversies, ideological hostilities, manufactured outrage, and carefully monetized distractions.

The spectacle changes... but the underlying questions concerning the concentration and exercise of power continues to remain.

Those who study the history of political authority understand that domination does not always require overt violence, nor does the erosion of autonomy necessarily announce itself through recognizable instruments of oppression.

Sometimes the most consequential transformations occur through the gradual normalization of arrangements that previous generations would have considered intolerable.

A population may become accustomed to surveillance when it is introduced as protection, accept behavioral manipulation when it is presented as personalization, and relinquish meaningful independence when dependence is marketed as convenience.

And the more indispensable these systems become, the more difficult it becomes to distinguish voluntary participation from practical necessity.

This is why the examination of concentrated power must extend beyond the personalities temporarily occupying political office and into the institutional, financial, technological, and informational structures that persist regardless of electoral outcomes.

Who possesses the information?

Who controls the infrastructure?

Who establishes the parameters within which decisions are made?

Who benefits from the increasing centralization of technological capabilities?

And who possesses the authority to investigate, challenge, or restrain those exercising such extraordinary influence?

These questions are not evidence of irrationality my friends... They are fundamental inquiries into the relationship between authority, accountability, and human freedom.

Because if history has demonstrated anything with an unmistakable consistency, it is that institutions possessing extraordinary power must never be presumed incapable of abusing it merely because they describe their objectives as benevolent.

A civilization cannot meaningfully defend freedoms it no longer understands, scrutinize institutions it has been conditioned to regard as infallible, or preserve its autonomy while remaining indifferent to the mechanisms through which its decisions are increasingly influenced.

The responsibility of an intellectually independent population is therefore not to accept every extraordinary explanation offered by those challenging established authority, nor to dismiss every uncomfortable question simply because powerful institutions insist that nothing warrants investigation.

It is to demand evidence, examine historical precedent, investigate conflicts of interest, expose demonstrable abuses, and refuse to confuse institutional prestige with unquestionable truth.

Because the ultimate danger is not simply that humanity might be deceived by those possessing extraordinary power.

It is that humanity might gradually become so accustomed to the conditions of its own dependence that it ceases to recognize the difference between genuine freedom and the carefully managed appearance of it.

And perhaps that is the most
important question of all...

If the boundaries of your choices, the information informing your beliefs, and the technological systems governing your existence are increasingly determined by institutions beyond your meaningful oversight, to what extent can you genuinely describe yourself as free?

Have you wondered if religious obligations are holding your heart captive instead of setting it free?

Do the struggles of daily life echo an ancient battle between slavery and promise?

What does it mean for you to live as a child of the free woman rather than the slave?

Dive into the allegory of Sarah and Hagar from Galatians 4 where the freedom Christ won calls you to stand firm.

Embracing the Freedom Christ Offers from Galatians 4

The passage from Galatians opens a window into the heart of Christian living by contrasting two paths that shape our relationship with God. It draws on the ancient story of Abraham to show how faith leads to true liberty rather than endless striving. Readers who seek to follow Christ yet sometimes stumble will find reassurance here because the focus remains on grace rather than perfection. This reflection explores the verses step by step so that the promise of freedom can settle into daily life with hope and clarity.

What Can Abraham's Two Sons Teach Us About Our Spiritual Heritage?

The first section of the reading recalls that Abraham had two sons one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. These mothers represent two covenants that guide human hearts in different directions. One covenant comes from Mount Sinai and leads to slavery while the other points toward the promise. The text explains that the son born of the slave woman was born according to the flesh yet the son of the free woman was born through the promise. This contrast helps believers see that their identity rests not on outward rules alone but on the inner call of God. When people try their best and still feel bound the story reminds them that the promise opens a wider way forward.

The deeper meaning surfaces when we notice how the slave woman corresponds to the present Jerusalem while the free woman corresponds to the Jerusalem above. That heavenly city is described as our mother and the reading quotes Isaiah to show that the barren one will rejoice with many children. Such imagery lifts the spirit because it promises growth and belonging even when earthly efforts fall short. The faithful can take comfort knowing that their spiritual lineage traces back to freedom rather than bondage. This heritage encourages continued trust in God who fulfills promises beyond human calculation.

Why Does the Heavenly Jerusalem Offer Us Lasting Freedom?

Moving through the verses the reading shifts attention to the city that is above and free. This Jerusalem stands as the true mother of all who believe and it invites participation in a liberty that earthly systems cannot provide. The quotation from Isaiah celebrates the one who was desolate yet now has more children than the one with a husband. That image speaks to renewal and unexpected joy for those who feel spiritually barren at times. By identifying with this heavenly reality believers discover strength to keep walking in faith even after setbacks.

The passage closes the section by declaring that we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman. This statement affirms dignity and belonging in a way that motivates steady effort without despair. People who aim to live well yet encounter weakness can rest in the knowledge that their status comes from promise rather than performance. The freedom described here is not license for selfishness but an open space in which love and goodness can flourish. Such freedom lifts the burden of constant self-justification and replaces it with grateful response to God.

How Do We Stand Firm in the Freedom Christ Has Given?

The final verses of the reading deliver the well-known line that for freedom Christ set us free so stand firm and do not submit again to the yoke of slavery. This sentence captures the core invitation of the entire passage and urges believers to protect the gift they have received. Standing firm does not mean never falling but rather returning quickly to the freedom already won. The yoke of slavery refers to any attempt to earn salvation through rigid observance alone rather than through trusting faith. When daily life brings moments of discouragement these words serve as a gentle reminder to choose liberty once more.

Living this freedom involves recognizing that Christ has already broken the chains that once held us. The reflection encourages readers to view their struggles through the lens of grace so that small failures do not define the whole journey. Instead each day becomes an opportunity to walk in the liberty that fosters genuine goodness. The message remains positive because it highlights what has been accomplished rather than what remains unfinished. By standing firm in this freedom the faithful discover renewed energy to serve others and grow in virtue.

In this way the reading from Galatians offers a steady call to embrace the freedom already given and to let that freedom shape every aspect of life.
May the peace of Christ be with you,

Happy Columbus Day: The Pledge That Still Anchors a Nation of Explorers

On October 12, 1892, millions of American schoolchildren stood in classrooms across the country and recited the Pledge of Allegiance for the first time in public schools. 

The occasion was the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’s landing in the New World. 

Written by Francis Bellamy and introduced as part of the National Public School Celebration, the pledge was a deliberate act of national unity—tying the fresh promise of American citizenship to the bold voyage that had opened the continent four centuries earlier. 

That moment in 1892 was not accidental. Organizers chose Columbus Day because they understood what the 1492 landing represented: the beginning of the European age of discovery that made the American experiment possible. 

When Columbus’s three ships made landfall on an island in the Bahamas—San Salvador, as he named it—he believed he had reached Asia. Instead, he connected the Atlantic world to the Americas, launching the Columbian Exchange of people, plants, ideas, and technologies that would eventually produce the freest and most prosperous nation in history.

The schoolchildren of 1892, reciting “I pledge allegiance to my Flag and the Republic for which it stands,” were being invited into that inheritance. 

They were told, in the plain language of a classroom oath, that the courage required to cross an unknown ocean in 1492 still lived in the American character. 

From the first permanent English settlements that followed Columbus’s routes, to the pioneers who pushed west, to the inventors, soldiers, and entrepreneurs who built an industrial and democratic superpower, the United States has repeatedly answered the same call: venture beyond the known map.

Columbus Day remains the natural day to honor that spirit. 

It commemorates not only one navigator’s calculated gamble, backed by the Spanish crown, but the larger tradition of discovery that defines the country.

It remembers the sailor who risked everything, the monarchs who financed the venture, the crews who endured it, and the long-term result: self-governing societies in the Western Hemisphere where opportunity and ordered liberty could take root. 

When those 1892 schoolchildren pledged allegiance, they were affirming that the Republic standing on that foundation was worth defending.

Every October 12 offers the same invitation. 

Fly the flag. 

Recall three small ships and a determined captain. 

Teach the next generation that the greatest nations are built by people willing to sail past the edge of the map—and that the pledge first spoken on this date still binds us to that same restless, confident purpose.

Happy Columbus Day.

Schoolchildren across the country stood and spoke the same words for the first time on this day in 1892.

Francis Bellamy, a former Baptist minister working for the magazine The Youth’s Companion wrote the Pledge of Allegiance that summer to mark the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’s landing. The magazine published it on September 8th and promoted it as the centerpiece of a nationwide public school celebration of Columbus Day.

President Benjamin Harrison had proclaimed the anniversary a national holiday and urged schools to use the occasion to teach the duties of citizenship. So on October 12th millions of students raised the flag and recited Bellamy’s original version. “I pledge allegiance to my Flag and the Republic for which it stands, one nation, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.”

The wording later changed. In the 1920s “my Flag” became “the Flag of the United States of America.” In 1954 Congress added the phrase “under God.” 

What began as a single coordinated exercise for schoolchildren has remained a daily patriotic ritual in American classrooms ever since.

text:
In a bout billed as "For the American Heavyweight Title" on October 13, 1931, at Ebbet's Field in Brooklyn, New York, Jack Sharkey gives Primo Carnera a drubbing winning a 15-round unanimous decision.

The United Press, which scored the bout 12-1-2 in rounds in favor of Sharkey, would write:

"Jack Sharkey and referee 'Gunboat' Smith shared credit today for providing the finest heavyweight fight since Jack Dempsey's unforgettable brawl with Luis Firpo. Sharkey did his part by thrashing Primo Carnera over a 15 round bout at Ebbets Field last night, and doing it so decisively that the "super man" myth surrounding the Italian was dissipated. However, had it not been for Smith, the fight would have ended in the 4th round with Sharkey winning on a technicality and 30,000 spectators robbed of the contest they paid $100,000 to witness. Sharkey, leading from the start and punishing his foe at will, floored the 261 lb. Italian with a smashing left hook to the jaw in the 4th. Primo was confused when he got off his back and on his knees. He pulled erect at the count of six, but hearing the shouts of his seconds urging him to take advantage of a full count he dropped back to his knees. Sharkey and his manager, Johnny Buckley shouted protests to Smith, claiming the bout on a foul because Primo went down without being hit--a rule violation punishable by DQ. Primo got up again, dropped to his knees a second time as Sharkey rushed forward, and finally came up at the count of eight. Smith urged Sharkey forward, but Jack ran to his corner and attempted to jump through the ropes. Sharkey then waived the foul claim and went back to fight. Encouraged by the knowledge that Carnera could be hurt, Sharkey blasted away with jolting left hooks to the head and body and went on to win as he pleased. The 15th was Sharkey's best round. He landed a terrific left hook to the chin as the round opened and for the remainder of the session drove Carnera about the ring." 

"You're a hell of a sight better than I thought, and plenty game." said Jack Sharkey to Primo Carnera afterwards.

Sharkey will win the Heavyweight Championship in his next bout, in June of 1932, with a rather controversial 15-round split decision over  titlist Max Schmeling. 

The German, of course, had won the title vacated by Gene Tunney with a controversial 4th round DQ of Sharkey.

The first Carnera-Sharkey fight comes up often when it comes to explaining Carnera's 6th round KO of Sharkey for the title just twenty months later.

Some believe the fight was fixed. 

The Associated Press reported: "Skeptics pointed to the shift in betting odds to 6 to 5 in Carnera's favor, shortly before the fight, marking the first time a title challenger ever had crawled through the ropes a favorite." 

However, according to the New York Times, the late money was actually skewed toward Sharkey. The Times reported that Carnera was a 6 to 5 favorite when Broadway bookies closed shop at 6 P.M. An hour later, bookies working the crowd were quoting Sharkey the favorite at odds of 7 to 5.

Sharkey (pictured separately) would deny, to his death, that he threw that fight. 

"I’d never have done anything like that. I was raised Catholic. I was raised to be honest," he said late in life. He added, "I was on top of the world. Why would I purposefully lose?"

Jack Sharkey, unfortunately for him, would be remembered mostly for his loss to Carnera, and is among the more "lost" or "forgotten" heavyweight titlists of the 20th century. 

He'd also retreat from public life, for the most part, following the end of his ring career which, perhaps, contributed to that.

From the obituary for Jack Sharkey, who had passed on August 17th, written in the Independent on August 20, 1994:

Joseph Paul Zukauskas (Jack Sharkey), boxer: born Binghampton, New York 26 October 1902; World Heavyweight Champion 1932-33; married (one son, two daughters); died Beverly, Massachusetts 17 August 1994.
JACK SHARKEY was one of the most temperamental, hot-headed heavyweights in boxing history - and also one of the finest.
Sharkey was world heavyweight champion between June 1932, when he won a controversial points verdict over Max Schmeling, of Germany, and June 1933, when he lost on an equally controversial knockout against Primo Carnera, of Italy.
He was unlucky to grow up as a a fighter during the Roaring Twenties when Jack Dempsey ruled the boxing world, reaching his peak when Dempsey and his successor Gene Tunney had gone, and boxing, like the world, had entered its Depression Years. There were still huge attendances at Sharkey's fights, but life wasn't the same after the Wall Street Crash of 1929. The greatest promoter of the time, Tex Rickard, died of peritonitis as the Twenties ended, and with his demise and the retirement of Dempsey, boxing died a little too.
History does not treat Sharkey kindly, for he reigned between the Dempsey years and the advent of the equally great Joe Louis. 
He was the only man to have fought them both. 
It was in New York in 1927 that he met Dempsey, who had just lost the heavyweight crown to Tunney. Sharkey outboxed and outfought the fabled Manassa Mauler for most of the first six rounds, but then his temper let him down. Dempsey landed a left hook Sharkey felt was below the belt. In his pain and anger Sharkey turned to complain to the referee - and Dempsey promptly flattened him with a left hook to the chin.
The oldest rule in boxing says 'protect yourself at all times'. Sharkey paid in pain and hard cash for breaking it. 
Dempsey went on to fight Tunney again in the celebrated fight that became known as the 'Battle of the Long Count' in Soldier Field, Chicago, while Sharkey was back in the queue with a multitude of others.
'I came home and I went in the hospital,' Sharkey recalled more than 40 years later, in Peter Heller's In This Corner (1973). 'I passed blood there for a long time . . . this is never brought out in print, the after-effects of a fight. You dry out like a lightweight, you're dehydrated, pains that you have, you come home you soak in a tub full of Epsom salts, the pain and the aches. No one knows what a fighter goes through after the fight.'
Sharkey fought his way back until, on Tunney's retirement, they matched him for the vacant title against Max Schmeling, in Yankee Stadium, New York, on 12 June 1930. 
The fight had hardly warmed up when Sharkey hit Schmeling low, the German crumpled in a heap and was carried to his corner by his seconds. The distraught and frustrated Sharkey was disqualified - and this is still the only time since bare-knuckle days that the heavyweight championship of the world has been won and lost on a foul. 
The outcome of that fight resulted in the introduction of the 'No Foul' rule in American boxing (so that a match cannot be won on a foul) - and led to the mandatory use of a foul-proof cup to cover a fighter's genitals.
To his dying day, Sharkey felt the result was a product of mob interference and that his final punch was legal: 'On (Schmeling's) end there was some dubious characters. So what, what can you do? Got a good payday, dollars 177,000. What the hell is the sense of crying about it?'
Mentally, the defeat affected him for a long time, but eventually, on 21 June 1932, he was matched with Schmeling again for the title in Long Island, New York.
This time it seemed as if Schmeling had won a boring fight on points, but the decision went to Sharkey. 
It took Sharkey a year to defend - and then it was against the mob-controlled Carnera, who had been fed a diet of fixed fights to build him into a contender. Sharkey had already beaten him once and was by far the superior fighter. Yet in the sixth round he was knocked out by a spectacular upper cut. The astonishing result led to suggestions that he had taken a dive. Sharkey's version was more macabre. He said he lost concentration when he had a vision of his former protege Ernie Schaaf, who had died after fighting Carnera four months earlier.
Very few believed his story. 
He admitted that even his wife 'had her doubts'. He told one boxing historian in the 1970s: 'I can convince you, but I can't convince 200 million people.'
That knocked the heart out of him and he had long faded out of contention when, at the age of 33, they offered him a fight with the rising star Joe Louis in New York in August 1936. He lost easily in three rounds. 'I just threw some kisses to the crowd, and that was my last fight, my son's eighth birthday, 1936.'
Sharkey was a loner in a tough business, although he was also a committed family man with a wife and three children through most of his boxing career.
He was born Joseph Zukauskas in 1902, the son of Lithuanian immigrants. He left the family home in New York when he was a teenager and after drifting awhile, joined the navy. Eventually, while on leave in Boston, he took a fight for dollars (100) and became a professional boxer. A promoter declared his Lithuanian name unusable and so he used Jack after Jack Dempsey and Sharkey from 'Sailor' Tom Sharkey, who fought Jim Jeffries to a 25-round decision for the heavyweight title in 1899.
'I was a hot-headed guy,' he admitted. 'You could never tell what I'd do . . . Half the time I didn't know what the hell I was doing anyway. If I got bad decisions, I'd go in a tantrum, might look like I was crying. They called me cry baby, they called me 'The Lispin' Lith', 'The Garrulous Gob' . . . But it didn't bother me as long as I got the pay cheque. Always deposited it before a fight in a Boston bank and when I got home it was credited to my account.'
He kept his money and was loved by his family, though he became increasingly reclusive in very old age. He spent most of his time with his thoughts and memories. 
In 1983, he was softly informed as he sat in his room that Jack Dempsey had died. He barely looked up, but muttered with a grim smile: 'I finally beat the son- of-a-bitch, didn't I?'
Jack Sharkey will be remembered with affection and respect. He was a strong man who earned his money and provided for his family in one of the hardest businesses of all.

In Shelby the training camp of Gibbons was set up very near the outdoor arena. While Tommy and his family stayed in a house provided for them, the rest of the entourage lived in two large tents at the training site. Gibbons put on daily training session for which he charged and so put a few exhibitions in nearby towns. Meanwhile, the promoters were unable to come up with Dempsey's second payment on $100,000 on the due date of June 1, making that installment in mid-June.
On June 28th the entire population of Shelby as well as out-of-town visitors filled the arena for the Shelby stampede and Blackfoot Indian show where Tommy Gibbons was to be made a member of the Blackfoot tribe. Tommy's wife, Helen and his children were in attendance for the ceremony. There were a lot of bucking broncos and hat-waving cowboys when the sound of tom-toms were heard. The show stopped at that point. A procession of Indians entered the area with Chief Curley Bear at the front and at his side, decked out in headdress, buckskin jacket, and legging heavy beaded with lots of color was Tommy Gibbons.
After marching the entire length of the grandstand, they moved to the middle of the arena where Chief Curley Bear spoke an Indian prayer calling on the gods to make Tom Gibbons strong and victorious. Gibbons was given the name "Thunder Chief." The ceremony concluded with Tommy shaking hands with all the braves as they crowded around him. Tommy was then taken back to the Indian village to change back into his clothes.
The group promoting the fight had relied on advance ticket sales to provide Dempsey's final $100,000 payment. They could not make it on time as they had only taken in $60,000 on the day it was due. In the early morning hours of July 2nd, Kearns called off the fight. The twenty-two special trains were immediately cancelled. A few hours later, Kearns changed his mind and decided to go through with the fight after had been paid what had been taken in. It was now too late to shave the show as the special trains could not be rescheduled and ticket orders from out-of-town ceased when word got out about Kearns calling off the fight.
At fight time the specially built Shelby Shell with 50,000 seats had a disappointing 7,202 paying customers. The gate was only $201,485 all of which went to Dempsey in advance. Several gate crashers had pushed their way into the arena and he surrounding hills were dotted with Indians taking in the fight. As the two fighters were in their corners, a man, a local oil man, was seen handing over several oil land leases to the Gibbons corner. Tommy Gibbons knew he was fighting for nothing but a chance to wing the heavyweight championship.
The Gibbons strategy was to keep Jack back on his heels by employing a powerful offense, not an easy task. During a wild exchange in the first round, Dempsey scored with a solid right that hurt Gibbons, forcing him to clinch until his head cleared. It was Jack's Sunday punch however, that Tommy was still there. Dempsey did not fight a clean fight at all as he attempted to score a knockout landing blows on separations on clinches as well as hitting Gibbons in the groin on several occasions, and there were no foul protectors in those days.
Gibbons more than held his own from the sixth through twelfth rounds with Dempsey coming on strong in the last three rounds to pull out the decision. Dempsey had not only not scored a knockout, he had failed to score even one knockdown and had to work to win the verdict. Tommy Gibbons had surprised everyone by taking Dempsey the entire fifteen rounds without really being hurt at any time. The town of Shelby had been seriously hurt as Dempsey and Kearns left the town bankrupt and broke.
On July 5th, Gibbons received a telegram from the Seattle office of the Pantages circuit offering him a fourteen week vaudeville engagement that would pay him $50,000. Gibbons later accepted the offer. Tommy did not leave Shelby empty-handed, however, even though he had received no purse money. He received $5,000 for training daily, $2,500 training expenses, $2,500 he charged fans for viewing his training sessions, and $5,000 for exhibitions in Conrad, Havre, and Great Falls, Montana, plus the oil land leases.
Tommy, his family and entourages returned to St. Paul on the morning of July 4th and on had to meet him on the railroad platform of the train depot were over 4,000 friends, admirers and fans. As the Oriental Limited pulled in they clogged not only the big depot building but spilled out onto Fourth Street. Gibbons was carried out of the building on the shoulders of some of the men there and when he appeared a loud cheer went up. One of the first to reach Gibbons was a childhood chum of his, Father T.E. Printon. Also on hand were the Governor, city and state politicians, businessmen, policemen, and of course, a host of relatives.
It was time for a parade though the city streets in a big car covered with flowers. An automobile moved along the streets both side were lined with adoring fans and people cheering from the windows of buildings along the route. Tommy and his wife were driven to their Garden Street home for a short period of time. Then they were off to the Town and Country Club for a breakfast attended by family members and close friends. After eating and a short talk to those at the club, it was off to St. Paul's Como Park where thousands more waited to see and hear Tommy. Next stop was the state capitol in a parade that extended nearly a mile. It was a show of total respect for Tommy Gibbons.
Gibbons was then taken off on his vaudeville tour with ring appearances but on the back burner. His next ring showing took place in St. Paul on January 15, 1924 which was a four round exhibition with another St. Paul great an former sparring partner Jimmy Delaney. The auditorium show was a benefit for the family of Tommy's old hometown rival and friend Billy Miske who had passed just two weeks before. Gibbons and Delaney wanted to be on this show as they both knew the Miske family well. The show drew a large house as other top pugilists like Pinkey and Richie Mitchell and Dago Joe Gans were also on the card. After expenses the promoters turned over $7,553 to Mrs. Miske.
Even though he hadn't bee active, Gibbons was still rated on top of the heavyweights when he had made his return in March of 1924. In a period of twenty days he knocked out Jack Moore, Joe Downey, Soldier Lee and Jack McFarland. A big match was arranged with French George Carpentier in Michigan City, Indiana for May 31st. A huge crowd of 30,000 filled the outdoor arena paying $250,000 to see the action. Tommy's purse for this appearance would be $61,781, his largest pay of his career at the time. Gibbons handled the Frenchman rather easily taking on a ten round newspaper decision over Carpentier.

COMMON SENSE FOR UNCOMMON CLAIMS

Chapter 5: The Lawsuit

By Thomas Plaine

After four chapters of political grudges, secret maps, liberal judges, and enough red string to gift-wrap the Governor’s Mansion, Robert Foster finally arrives at the courthouse. At last! Evidence will be required. This is unfortunate for several characters in our story, particularly Inference, who has been impersonating Evidence since the Prologue.

THE GOVERNOR DIDN’T ANSWER

Following the Supreme Court’s Callais decision, Foster wanted Governor Tate Reeves to call a special legislative session and eliminate the DeSoto judicial subdistrict. The DeSoto County Board of Supervisors requested action. Reeves didn’t call the requested session. Foster interprets this as evidence of a deliberate effort to protect an unconstitutional district.

Thomas Plaine offers another possibility: The Governor didn’t agree with Robert Foster. Admittedly, this explanation lacks the production values of a statewide conspiracy.

ENTER THE SECRETARY OF STATE

Foster tells us that Secretary of State Michael Watson privately encouraged the lawsuit and indicated he wouldn’t fight it. An interesting conversation. Unfortunately, Thomas Plaine wasn’t invited. Nor have we been furnished a recording, transcript, or commemorative photograph.

Then Foster sued Watson, along with Reeves, Fitch, and other state defendants. And the defendants opposed his requested injunction. Betrayal! Or, alternatively, a defendant defending an enacted state law in federal court. We mustn’t rush to conclusions.

THE FRIENDLY LAWSUIT

Foster apparently hoped this would be a relatively straightforward legal proceeding. Get a good lawyer. File the lawsuit. Present the evidence. Obtain an injunction. Fix the election. Everybody goes home.

He hired Mike Hurst, a former Trump-appointed U.S. Attorney and Mississippi Republican Party chairman. Foster describes Hurst’s willingness to take the case at a substantially reduced fee. Thomas Plaine respects lawyers who work for less money. He understands they are endangered in several jurisdictions.

But Foster’s optimism presents an interesting problem. He sued to change an election in which candidates had already qualified, spent money, and begun campaigning. He also challenged a district whose boundaries affected voters and organizations with their own legal interests. Some of those people were rather unlikely to respond: “Splendid! Please rearrange our election immediately. No objections whatsoever.”

AND THEN CAME THE ACLU

Civil-rights organizations intervened. A judicial candidate intervened. The State opposed the injunction. Suddenly Foster’s hoped-for straightforward lawsuit had become an actual lawsuit. With lawyers. And arguments. And people who disagreed with him. The horror.

Foster portrays these developments as further evidence of an establishment alliance. But the existence of several parties opposing the same requested injunction does not prove they negotiated a secret political bargain. It proves they disagreed with the plaintiffs’ requested relief. Thomas Plaine recognizes this is a disappointing plot twist.

THE CLOCK IS TICKING

Foster also suggests state officials deliberately delayed action until election deadlines made judicial intervention difficult. That is a serious claim about motive. There is, however, an inconvenient calendar. Callais was decided April 29. Foster filed suit July 2. That’s 64 days. Judge Aycock later considered the plaintiffs’ delay an important factor in denying emergency relief. The clock, it seems, was not exclusively operated from the Governor’s Mansion.

THE CHAPTER 5 LEDGER

The Legislature enacted the district. True. 

Foster believed Callais rendered it unconstitutional. True. 

Reeves did not call the special session Foster wanted. True. 

Foster hired counsel and filed a federal lawsuit. True. 

Other parties intervened and opposed his requested injunction. True.

text:
St. Edward, King of England
Confessor
October 13th

“This glorious saint... [was of] the ancient branch of the kings of Wessex... the Anglo-Saxons... Evangelized by Rome... remembered... whence their salvation had come... [In 800 A.D.], Egbert, a descendant of Cerdic, had gone on pilgrimage to Rome, when a deputation from the West Saxons offered him the crown, beside the tomb of the Prince of the apostles, at whose feet Charlemagne, at that very time, was restoring the empire. As Egbert united... the 7 kingdoms, so St. Edward, his last descendant, represents today in his own person the glorious holiness of them all.

Nephew to St. Edward the Martyr, [his reign]... of 24 years was one of the happiest England has ever known. Alfred the Great had no more illustrious imitator. The Danes, so long masters, now entirely subjugated within the kingdom, and without, held at bay by the noble attitude of the prince; Macbeth, the usurper of the Scotch throne, vanquished in a campaign that Shakespeare has immortalized; St. Edward’s Laws... [made] the basis of the British constitution; the saint’s munificence towards all noble enterprises, while at the same time he diminished the taxes: all this proves with sufficient clearness, that the sweetness of virtue, which made him the intimate friend of St. John the beloved disciple, is not incompatible with the greatness of a monarch.

Edward, surnamed the Confessor, nephew to St. Edward king & martyr, was the last king of the Anglo-Saxon race. Our Lord had revealed that he would one day be king, to a holy man named Brithwald. When Edward was 10... the Danes, who were devastating England, sought his life; he was therefore obliged to go into exile, to the court of his uncle the duke of Normandy. Amid the vices & temptations of the Norman court, he grew up pure & innocent, a subject of admiration to all... [with] pious devotion towards God & holy things... He was of a very gentle disposition, and so great a stranger to ambition that he was wont to say he would rather forego the kingdom than take possession of it by violence & bloodshed.

On the death of the tyrants who had murdered his brothers & seized their kingdom, he was recalled to his country, and ascended the throne to the greatest satisfaction & joy of all his subjects. He then applied himself to remove all traces of the havoc wrought by the enemy... he built many churches, and restored others, endowing them with rents & privileges... [eager] to see religion, which had been neglected, flourishing again. All writers assert that, though compelled by his nobles to marry, both he & his bride preserved their virginity intact... he was one day permitted to see our Lord in the Mass, shining with heavenly light & smiling upon him. His lavish charity won him the name of the father of orphans & of the poor; and he was never so happy as when he had exhausted the royal treasury on their behalf.

He was honored with the gift of prophecy, and foresaw much of England’s future history... when Sweyn, king of Denmark, was drowned in the very act of embarking on his fleet to invade England, Edward was supernaturally aware of the event the very moment it happened. He had a special devotion to St. John the evangelist, and was accustomed never to refuse anything asked in his name. One day St. John appeared to him as a poor man begging an alms... the king, having no money about him, took off his ring & gave it to him. Soon afterwards the saint sent the ring back to Edward, with a message that his death was at hand. The king then ordered prayers to be said for himself; and died most piously on the day foretold by St. John, the Nones of January... 1066. In the following century Pope Alexander III enrolled him, famous for miracles, among the saints. Innocent XI ordered his memory to be celebrated by the whole Church with a public Office... his body... [was] found incorrupt & exhaling a sweet fragrance.”

(The Liturgical Year, 1841-1875, Dom Prosper Guéranger)

By: Dr.s Jill Glasspool Malone and Robert W. Malone

“In fourteen hundred ninety-two, Columbus sailed the ocean blue.”
In the 1960s, when I was a child in elementary school, California was enjoying its golden years. Agriculture was thriving, vast cattle ranches still dotted the arid landscape, and the aerospace industry was reaching extraordinary heights. Hollywood was the undisputed capital of American moviemaking, and the state’s population and economy were growing by leaps and bounds. Brand new, uncrowded freeways made it easy to get around. California represented the best and brightest of America, a place of opportunity, innovation, ambition, and seemingly limitless possibilities. People from around the world looked to California as a symbol of what America could accomplish. There was a palpable sense of optimism about the future, a belief that hard work, ingenuity, and determination could make almost anything possible.

I grew up in Goleta, on California’s Central Coast, where Spanish heritage was woven into the landscape, the architecture, the place names, and the history we learned in school. We studied the Spanish missions, the California vaqueros, the great ranchos, and the Chumash Indians who had inhabited the region long before Europeans arrived. We learned about the hardships and injustices experienced by the Chumash, but we also learned about the explorers, missionaries, ranchers, and settlers who shaped California. I remember reading Richard Henry Dana Jr.’s Two Years Before the Mast, with its vivid descriptions of life aboard a sailing ship and the California coast in the 1830s. These stories brought our local history to life. They gave us an appreciation for the people who came before us, the hardships they endured, and the extraordinary changes that had transformed California into the place we called home.
And, of course, we learned American history. We learned about Christopher Columbus and his three small ships, the Niña, the Pinta, and the Santa María, sailing across the vast Atlantic in 1492. We learned about Spain’s role in the voyages of discovery, the European settlement of the Americas, the thirteen colonies, the American Revolution, and the founding of the United States. These stories were taught with a sense of wonder and pride. We were encouraged to admire the courage of explorers, the determination of pioneers, and the extraordinary accomplishments of the men and women who helped build this nation. We learned that America was a land of opportunity, a country founded on the ideals of liberty and self-government, and a place where ordinary people could aspire to extraordinary things.
That education gave us something important. It gave us a connection to our history, a sense of belonging, and pride in the country we had inherited. It taught us that America was worth appreciating, worth defending, and worth improving. It gave us patriotism, not as a political slogan or an obligation imposed from above, but as something that grew naturally from learning about the people, events, sacrifices, and achievements that had made our country possible.

The Columbus I learned about in elementary school was a navigator who crossed an immense ocean in three small wooden ships, undertaking a voyage whose outcome was anything but certain. We memorized the familiar rhyme, learned the names of the ships, and imagined what it must have been like to sail westward into waters that few Europeans had ever crossed. We were also taught about the people who already inhabited the Americas, the Spanish missions, and the hardships and injustices of colonization. We were instructed to read “Ishi in two worlds,” the heartrending story of one of the last remaining Native Californians to grow up outside the surrounding Anglo-Spanish-American culture. What began as a magazine publication has grown into a substantial educational enterprise, supported by the Pulitzer Center, with more than 100 curricular resources, a national network of more than 400 educators across 30 states, professional-development conferences, and classroom materials extending from elementary school through law school. This is no longer simply a controversial interpretation of American history. It is an organized effort to influence how American history is taught, supported by educational institutions, philanthropic funding, and a major national teachers’ union. The concern is not that children are learning about slavery, which is an essential part of American history, but that a contested interpretation placing racial oppression at the center of America’s origins is being promoted as a foundational framework for understanding the country and its institutions.

The Pulitzer Center identifies Meta, Open Society Foundations, Rockefeller Brothers Fund, and several other philanthropic organizations among supporters of its 1619 education initiative

California’s own Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum directs attention toward colonialism, systemic oppression, and social transformation. Educational organizations publish elementary-school lessons encouraging children to reconsider the celebration of Columbus. These are not imaginary controversies invented by political commentators. The materials are publicly available, and their authors openly describe the changes in historical interpretation they seek to promote.

There is an important difference between teaching children that Columbus and America’s founders were imperfect men, sometimes responsible for grave injustices, and teaching American history through an interpretive framework in which exploitation and oppression occupy the center of the national story. The first expands historical understanding. The second raises legitimate questions about how the nation’s achievements, founding ideals, and historical failures are weighed against one another. What children learn to admire, what they learn to condemn, and what they learn to regard as their national inheritance will influence how they understand the country in which they live.

And what are the results of this re-educational programming?

📷

The generational divide is striking. According to Gallup’s analysis of surveys conducted between 2021 and 2025, only 41 percent of Generation Z adults described themselves as extremely or very proud to be American, compared with 75 percent of Baby Boomers and 83 percent of the Silent Generation. These numbers raise an important question about the relationship between what children are taught and how they eventually regard their country. For generations, American schools emphasized the nation’s founding ideals, its achievements, and the responsibilities of citizenship, alongside its historical failures. American schools taught Americanism, a belief in the greatness of America.

The change extends beyond national pride. A September 2020 Pew Research Center survey found that 86 percent of Black adults believed America had not done enough to secure racial equality, up from 78 percent just a year earlier. Nearly two-thirds reported recently educating themselves about the history of racial inequality.

In 2020, 86% of black and Hispanic adults said that the country hasn’t done enough to address racial inequality.

📷

These findings emerged during a period of intense national conflict over race and reflect a growing emphasis on racial identity and historical injustice. They also raise a question worth examining: whether educational approaches that increasingly organize American history around racial divisions help students understand and overcome those divisions, or risk reinforcing them.

Today, most educational programs place considerably greater emphasis on systemic oppression, racial injustice, and the shortcomings of American institutions. There is no question that the shift has contributed to the growing generational divide in national pride.

The generational divide is unmistakable. Gallup found that only 41 percent of Generation Z adults are extremely or very proud to be American, compared with 75 percent of Baby Boomers. YouGov polling also shows that younger Americans are far more likely to view Christopher Columbus unfavorably than their grandparents. These surveys reveal a profound shift in how younger generations regard their country and its historical figures. When schools change the way American history is taught, it is reasonable to ask whether they are also changing how children understand what it means to be American.

Children begin forming attitudes about race, identity, and belonging long before they are capable of critically evaluating complicated historical arguments. Developmental research shows that racial attitudes emerge in early childhood and are shaped by the messages children receive from adults, peers, and institutions. This places an enormous responsibility on schools. Teaching any child to judge classmates through inherited categories of racial guilt or victimhood will reinforce the very prejudices education should help overcome.

When Racial Justice Became an Industry

The death of George Floyd in May 2020 ignited a wave of anger that swept across the United States. The educational philosophy known as critical pedagogy was heavily influenced by Paulo Freire, a Brazilian socialist educator whose work drew extensively on Marxist theories of oppression and class struggle. Freire believed schools should do more than teach facts and practical skills. Education should encourage students to question established institutions, identify perceived systems of oppression, and become agents of social and political change. His ideas have become influential in American universities and schools of education and helped shape approaches to teaching that emphasize social justice and political consciousness. The controversy over Christopher Columbus is no longer simply about a fifteenth-century explorer. One lesson introduces Columbus through navigation, maritime exploration, the dangers of the Atlantic crossing, and the extraordinary consequences of 1492.

Another begins by asking students to reconsider whether Columbus deserves to be celebrated or even remembered, emphasizing conquest, enslavement, and the experiences of Indigenous peoples. Both subjects belong in a serious history curriculum, but the choice of emphasis matters, particularly for young children who are still developing their understanding of history, identity, and national belonging.

The American founders understood the dangers of concentrated political power and unchecked majority rule. They established a representative republic with divided powers, constitutional limitations, and protections for individual liberty. These institutions were imperfectly applied from the beginning, but they also provided mechanisms through which later generations fought to abolish slavery, expand citizenship, and secure civil rights. Wes, the problem with your argument is neatly encapsulated in your assertion that your premise “will always be confirmed because it cannot be otherwise”.

You’ve constructed a premise that you declare incapable of falsification, then treat individual examples as confirmation of its universal truth. That’s circular reasoning, not logical necessity.

And there’s an obvious difficulty with your argument in the very Tennessee case you’re citing.

The defence expressly offered to respect Lee’s female identity and use she/her pronouns while also presenting evidence of her biological sex. The two were plainly not considered mutually exclusive.

The error identified by the appellate court was the exclusion of relevant evidence, not the recognition of Lee’s gender identity. You’re conflating those two things and extrapolating from one erroneous judicial ruling to the supposed inevitable corruption of every institution that recognises transgender people.

And now you’re attempting to draw a symmetry between a completed criminal trial, examined on appeal, and early newspaper coverage of an entirely separate incident.

In Tennessee, we have a judicial ruling found erroneous on appeal, resulting in a retrial.

In Chicago, we have a newspaper reporting criminal allegations and quoting an activist’s interpretation of the circumstances. That interpretation has no judicial authority whatsoever.

You could read the same incident reported in two different newspapers and find markedly different emphases, quotations and narratives. We see that routinely in the UK. That’s editorial selection, not evidence of judicial corruption.

You may reasonably criticise the Tribune’s editorial choices, but how does that establish your proposition that transgender recognition necessarily corrupts institutional standards?

You claim an ocean of evidence, yet you’re selecting examples from fundamentally different contexts and declaring both confirmation of a conclusion you’ve already decided must be true.

That’s not logical necessity. It’s confirmation bias.

Lowenthal said, “California must make meaningful progress to train Californians on the danger of hate speech not only in the workplaces, but in society as a whole.”

This is why California’s law should concern the church and everyone else, for that matter. When state officials declare the state needs to train society on what is appropriate speech, all of society is in trouble. California is not merely a laboratory for the Left; it is a warning to the rest of America. The question for voters is whether California’s experiment stops at the state line, or comes to Washington. And the question for the church is even more fundamental: when government demands that we compromise biblical truth, will we have the courage of Peter and John to stand firm and speak it?

Lightweight prospect Bobby Scanlon (pictured) goes to 30-0-1 with a 10-round unanimous decision over Gale Kerwin at Madison Square Garden on July 18, 1958.

From boxrec on Bobby Scanlon, 42-12-1 with 12 KO wins, active from 1954-66:

Bobby Scanlon had a very difficult childhood growing up in Father Baker's orphanage. Possessing choirboy looks, Scanlon was frequently the target of tougher kids. Scanlon turned to boxing and became the orphanage champion. He began his pro career in mid 1954. During the first three-and-a-half years of his career, he was undefeated in 32 fights, at 31-0-1. He competed mainly in New York City, with occasional stops in Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse and Erie, Pennsylvania.
His sister, Carol, remembers her brother driving his powder-blue Thunderbird around the First Ward. He is also remembered as a very generous brother who returned home during the Christmas season to buy gifts for his sisters.
Bobby Scanlon's manager, Mike Scanlon (no relation), then moved Bobby and his other three fighters--Rocky Fumerelle, Richie Todaro and Joey Giambra--to San Francisco in 1957. After a brief stay Todaro returned to Buffalo. The remaining three fighters occupied the same house along with Mike Scanlon, and they all became top contenders in their divisions. Scanlon improved his winning streak to 32 in California. He defeated such top fighters as Lauro Salas, Wallace (Bud) Smith, Joey Lopes and Dave Gallardo.
Following the March 1957 fight with Davy Gallardo, Scanlon broke with his manager Mike Scanlon. Bobby was already showing a dislike for the tough training techniques utilized by Mike. His contract was purchased by Art Benjamin, and later by Nick Kobseff and Lou Sabella. Fred Apostoli, former middleweight champion, would later become Bobby Scanlon's trainer.
According to Rocky Fumerelle, "Bobby Scanlon was his own worst enemy." Scanlon was good-looking and a good fighter. He was very popular among the Irish of San Francisco. If he would have remained in better shape and maintained a regular training schedule, "I have little doubt that Bobby Scanlon would have been the Lightweight champion of the world."
From late 1958 to early 1960 Scanlon not only saw his winning streak come to an end, but he also lost five of seven fights. Scanlon's winning streak came to an end when he suffered a third-round knockout to Paolo Rosi. Prior to this fight Scanlon was rated third in the Lightweight Division behind Rosi and Carlos Ortiz. Soon after his initial loss to Rosi, Scanlon lost another ten-round decision to Paolo. Scanlon also lost a pair of ten-round decisions to Johnny Gonsalves, as well as a decision to Al Urbina. But Scanlon did win a big ten-round decision over Orlando Zulueta.
Scanlon then returned to Buffalo to fight fellow Buffalonian Jackie Donnelly. In a hard-fought 12-round fight, Scanlon won the New York State Lightweight championship. It was one of Scanlon's biggest paydays, as he collected $4,937 for the fight.
Following the first Johnny Gonsalves fight, Scanlon began to suffer double vision. It got worse as he prepared for the second fight with Gonsalves. The problem continued through the Jackie Donnelly fight, as well as an August fight with Francisco Santos. Scanlon laid off from boxing for a year before he returned to fighting again in 1962. Things were not the same. In addition to the double vision, Scanlon had suffered a serious kidney and liver infection. He changed managers four times, and saw his level of competition go down, losing seven of his last thirteen fights.
Although Scanlon was fighting less frequently in 1965 and 1966, he was still experiencing eye problems. He retired from boxing in mid-1966. After he retired from the ring everything went downhill. Early in his boxing career Scanlon had been offered a job in public relations with the Oakland Raiders football team, but now there were few job offers. Although he became deeply religious, his physical and mental health began to deteriorate. Scanlon was struggling to adjust to life without boxing, struggling to restore some meaning to his life, when he died in a fire at the Hotel Lackawanna on June 23, 1975. He was only 39 years old. His final record was 42-12-1.
